label: Reading the news tip
items: Read past the headline: the first paragraph often changes the meaning.
Check the date on a story. Old news is often reshared as new.
Find the original source: the study, the document or the full video.
Compare two outlets with different viewpoints before forming an opinion on a big story.
Ask "compared to what?" when you see a percentage.
A single poll is a snapshot. Look at several, and at the margin of error.
Strong emotion is a signal to slow down and check before you share.
Photos can be real but from another time or place. Search where they first appeared.
Follow fewer sources and read them properly instead of scrolling everything.
Turn off most news notifications; keep only real safety alerts.
Corrections matter: trustworthy outlets publish them clearly.
"Experts say" without a name or credentials is a warning sign.
Correlation is not causation: ask what else could explain both things.
Averages hide the spread. Ask for the median and the range.
Before the weekend, check the 7-day forecast and plan the outdoor day for the best weather.
Satire sites exist. If a story sounds absurd, check whether the site is a joke.
Local news is often the most useful news for your actual week.
A good routine: weather, three headlines, one topic you care about, then stop.
Wikipedia's current events portal is a calm summary of the day, with links to sources.
Notice what a story leaves out, not just what it says.
Charts: check the axis starts at zero before believing a dramatic slope.
Breaking news is often revised within hours. Waiting for the daily summary can be more accurate.
Reading history for five minutes a day builds context that makes today's news make sense.
Share the article, not just the headline screenshot, so friends can see the context.
If something confirms exactly what you already believe, check it twice.
Ask who benefits from you believing a claim.
Fact-checkers such as Reuters, AFP and Snopes publish how they checked, not just the verdict.
Take a news-free walk once a week. The world will still be there.
Check three things on any website: who runs it, how they make money, and how they fix errors.
Keep a short list of reliable sources and visit them directly rather than through feeds.
